papers.title: Immunomodulatory RIG-I Agonist SLR14 Confers Protection Against a Range of Highly Pathogenic Negative Sense RNA viruses
papers.abstract: Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic RNA viruses, including filoviruses, henipaviruses and Rift Valley Fever virus (RVFV), pose a significant threat to human health. Due to their epidemic potential and high pathogenicity, these viruses are categorized as WHO priority pathogens, yet we still lack effective medical countermeasures (MCMs) against most of these dangerous pathogens, supporting that host-directed antivirals will be advantageous for broadly acting MCMs. Here we assessed the antiviral efficacy of SLR14, an immunomodulatory stem-loop RNA that activates RIG-I, for its activity against a panel of highly pathogenic viruses. SLR14 treatment provided broad-spectrum protection, markedly reducing infection with Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus, and Sudan virus in human primary monocyte-derived macrophages, and Nipah virus replication in iPSC-derived endothelial cells, whether administered prophylactically or therapeutically. In vivo, a single dose of SLR14 protected mice against lethal RVFV infection when administered prophylactically, and, notably, retained significant efficacy when administered up to two days post-infection. Therapeutic SLR14 administration also improved survival rates of EBOV-infected mice. Although EBOV infection and SLR14 treatment activated overlapping innate immune pathways in human macrophages, viral infection induced a nonprotective response, whereas SLR14 elicited a well-regulated, markedly stronger and protective interferon-stimulated and inflammatory gene signature while avoiding prolonged IFN gene upregulation. Our data identify SLR14 as a potent host-directed therapeutic with broad antiviral efficacy against some of the most lethal viral pathogens.

papers.title: Predicted structure of the 89-kDa invasion-tip protein of Holospora obtusa, an endonuclear symbiont of Paramecium caudatum, suggests a pH-dependent conformational change
papers.abstract: The endonuclear symbiont Holospora obtusa invades the macronucleus of Paramecium caudatum using an infectious-form invasion-tip containing a major 89-kDa periplasmic protein implicated in escape from the host digestive vacuole and macronuclear invasion. Sequence-based analyses placed this protein within a Holospora-specific family and predicted an N-terminal membrane-anchoring module and a long alpha-helical C-terminal region. AlphaFold2 modeling followed by molecular dynamics indicated that the C-terminal region forms an antiparallel, spectrin-repeat-like helical solenoid containing a localized three-helix coiled-coil. The protein exhibits a large pH-dependent charge difference, becoming 55 units more positive at pH 4 than at pH 7. Independent simulations at these pH values differed mainly in the relative orientation of the N-terminal core and C-terminal rod, described by DynDom as an approximately 35 degrees rigid-body rotation about a hinge centered on Gly291. However, none of the nearby glutamates (Glu273, Glu275, and Glu302) formed a pH-dependent salt bridge, and no specific protonation-dependent interaction responsible for the conformational difference was identified. We nonetheless propose, as a testable hypothesis, that acidification of the digestive vacuole may promote this reorientation, thereby repositioning the N-terminal membrane-anchoring module at the bacterial surface as an early step toward escape from the vacuole.

papers.title: Exchange of metabolic pathway intermediates as the origin for metabolite cross-feeding interactions in E. coli auxotrophic co-cultures
papers.abstract: A large fraction of microbes in natural environments are auxotrophs that rely on metabolite exchange for growth. The Black Queen hypothesis and related frameworks explain gene loss and reliance on shared metabolites. Yet it is not fully understood how metabolite cross-feeding emerges and gives rise to experimentally observable community performance. Here, we propose that exchange of biosynthetic pathway intermediates provides a mechanistic route for the emergence of metabolite cross-feeding. Building on prior work demonstrating intermediate exchange in E. coli auxotrophs, we investigated co-cultures between a methionine auxotroph ({Delta}metA) and a panel of histidine auxotrophs. Among these, only {Delta}hisD exhibited efficient co-culture growth with {Delta}metA, suggesting a unique role for the final step of histidine biosynthesis, which converts histidinol to histidine. We found that {Delta}metA-{Delta}hisD co-cultures accumulated high levels of extracellular histidinol (>200 M), suggesting a mechanism for metabolite exchange. Spent media from these co-cultures supported growth of all histidine auxotrophs except {Delta}hisD, confirming that histidinol, rather than histidine, was the dominant exchanged metabolite. Furthermore, we observed that {Delta}metA efficiently converted histidinol to histidine only under methionine-limited conditions, suggesting that nutrient limitation promoted overflow of converted histidine to the extracellular environment. To quantitatively assess whether histidinol exchange could account for the observed co-culture behavior, we constructed a mechanistic model that links extracellular histidinol dynamics to co-culture growth through independently measured conversion capacity of the {Delta}metA strain. Rather than fitting growth empirically, we used experimentally derived parameters to predict co-culture growth from the measured histidinol-to-histidine conversion flux. The model accurately recapitulated the timing and magnitude of growth and population dynamics, supporting the idea that accumulation of histidinol enabled the conversion-driven supply of histidine that sustained {Delta}hisD, while coupling growth between the two strains. Taken together, these results suggest that metabolite cross-feeding in syntrophic co-cultures can emerge from the accumulation of pathway intermediates and their conditional conversion under nutrient limitation, providing a plausible mechanism for the rapid establishment of mutualistic interactions.

papers.title: Insights Into an Antibacterial Type VI Membrane-Disrupting Effector Of Adherent Invasive Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Adherent Invasive Escherichia coli (AIEC) strains are associated with ileal Crohn's disease and may contribute to intestinal dysbiosis through antibacterial competition. The AIEC reference strain LF82 encodes two type VI secretion systems (T6SSs), a contractile machine that injects an effector-loaded needle made of Hcp, VgrG and PAAR into neighbouring rivals, favoring niche colonization. LF82 T6SSs harbour several putative antibacterial toxin-immunity modules. Here we characterize the T6SS-1 encoded TmeAIEC, a PAAR-fused T6SS effector carrying a C-terminal Tme domain, hallmark of Tme (Type VI membrane disrupting effector) toxins, and its DUF1240-like immunity protein TmiAIEC. When heterologously produced in E. coli K-12 as well as in E. coli and Citrobacter clinical isolates, TmeAIEC is toxic only upon periplasmic targeting, and its toxicity is neutralized by TmiAIEC. Periplasmically-targeted TmeAIEC inserts into the inner membrane, collapses the proton motive force and increases cell permeability, consistent with a membrane-disrupting activity. Mutational analyses coupled to functional assays identified a predicted hydrophobic transmembrane segment and a conserved aspartate residue within the Tme domain as key determinants for TmeAIEC toxicity. These findings establish TmeAIEC/TmiAIEC as a functional T6SS toxin-immunity pair and reveal conserved determinants underlying the activity of Tme-family membrane-disrupting effectors.

papers.title: The porin MspA is a phage-specific determinant of mycobacteriophage infection
papers.abstract: Mycobacteriophages are being developed as therapeutics for mycobacterial infections, but their highly variable host ranges limit this application and the bacterial factors that determine whether infection succeeds remain poorly defined. The determinants characterized so far are dominated by cell envelope lipids and glycolipids. Here, we performed a genome-wide CRISPRi screen in Mycobacterium smegmatis to identify host functions associated with susceptibility to BPs{Delta}33HTH HRM10. After prolonged phage challenge, the outer membrane porin genes mspA and mspC were among the most strongly enriched hits, whereas the closely related paralogs mspB and mspD were not enriched despite sharing high amino-acid identity across the family. Deletion of mspA or mspC reduced BPs{Delta}33HTH HRM10 plaque formation and produced smaller, more turbid plaques, with the stronger phenotype following loss of mspA, the major outer membrane porin of M. smegmatis. Across a panel of 25 mycobacteriophages, 11 showed either a more than tenfold reduction in titer or loss of discrete plaque formation on {Delta}mspA, while the remainder were largely unaffected. These findings identify outer membrane porins as phage-dependent determinants of mycobacterial susceptibility, revealing an additional layer of specificity in phage infection beyond previously characterized cell envelope lipids and glycolipids.

papers.title: Non-canonical alternate interactors of SARS CoV-2 Spike protein implicated in placental susceptibilty
papers.abstract: Vertical transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is controversial. Owing to the low expression of ACE2 along with TMPRSS2 in placenta, role of secondary receptors becomes significant. In our study we predicted twelve interactors of spike protein expressed in placenta through interactome analysis followed by docking and molecular dynamic simulation. Three interactors of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein were found to be CD147, EGFR and LDLR. Expression at transcriptomic and translational level by real-time PCR and immunohistochemistry respectively was observed in placenta samples obtained from women with COVID exposure risk and compared to control. Elevated protein levels of CD147 (OR=14.667), ACE2 (OR=8.25) and LDLR (OR=1.9) was associated with higher exposure risk. However, the variation in mRNA expression was not statistically significant. Computational study showed that CD147/basigin, EGFR and LDLR stably interact with spike protein outside its primary receptor binding domain. In-vitro binding assay confirmed the physical interaction between spike protein and the placental receptors. In-silico site-directed mutagenesis further identified key potential binding hotspots of spike protein- Tyr28 and Trp64 for CD147, Phe643, Val642, Thr632 for LDLR and Leu8, Phe59, Phe32, Tyr28, Trp64, Trwp152, His245, and Val213 for EGFR. Finally, concluded that CD147, EGFR and LDLR might act as secondary non-canonical cofactors for SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in placenta, thereby increasing its susceptibility and tissue tropism. The study overall gives a better insight into potential placental suscpetibility providing targeted therapeutic opportunities.

papers.title: TonB-dependent Transporters of Fe-petrobactin in Marinobacter nauticus and Southern Ocean bacteria
papers.abstract: TonB-dependent transporters (TBDTs) play a central role in siderophore-mediated iron acquisition in the marine environment. However, assigning substrate specificity to TBDTs remains a major bottleneck in understanding the ecological and mechanistic roles of siderophore production and uptake. Here, we identify in Marinobacter nauticus two TBDTs, OptA and OptB, that share low sequence identity yet both mediate Fe-petrobactin uptake. Despite this functional overlap, they underlie distinct regulatory mechanisms, suggesting differential utilization under specific environmental conditions. Phylogenetic analyses indicate that OptA likely co-evolved with the petrobactin biosynthetic gene cluster, whereas OptB appears to have followed a distinct evolutionary trajectory, acquiring the capacity to import petrobactin as a xenosiderophore. Using resuscitated communities from the Southern Ocean, we further show that Fe-petrobactin stimulated prokaryotic growth. Based on amino acid similarity, we identified OptB-like transporters encoded in metagenomes and MAGs and show that taxa harbouring these transporters, such as Pseudoaltermonas, respond specifically to Fe-petrobactin addition. OptB-like transporters were also detected in environmental metagenomes from the Southern Ocean, whereas the petrobactin biosynthetic gene clusters were not, indicating that petrobactin primarily functions as a xenosiderophore in natural communities.

papers.title: Transcriptomics uncovers outer membrane remodeling as conserved strategy for Burkholderia cenocepacia survival in protozoan and macrophage phagosomes
papers.abstract: Bacterivorous protists expose bacteria to hostile stress conditions that resemble those encountered within macrophage phagosomes and may therefore act as training grounds for bacterial pathogens. However, the mechanisms enabling bacterial survival within protozoan phagosomes remain poorly understood. Here we characterized the transcriptome of the opportunistic pathogen Burkholderia cenocepacia during transit through phagosomes and expelled food vacuoles of the ubiquitous protozoan ciliate Tetrahymena elliotti. Our data revealed a coordinated response involving bacterial metabolic reprogramming, with the upregulation of NADPH-generating pathways and host nutrient uptake systems, alongside the activation of several stress responses and envelope remodeling to maintain outer membrane barrier function and repair phagosomal damage. Disruption of antioxidant defenses, the RpoE-dependent envelope stress response, the Mla pathway and other proteins required for outer membrane integrity severely impaired intracellular survival in both protozoa and macrophages, revealing conserved mechanisms required for persistence within evolutionarily distant phagocytes. This adaptive response not only contributed to survival but it also primed B. cenocepacia for increased chlorhexidine resistance and adhesion to collagen and human lung epithelial cells. Collectively, our findings reveal that protozoan phagosomes drive physiological adaptations with consequences extending beyond grazing resistance. Protozoa may therefore disseminate stress-adapted bacteria with enhanced resistance and colonization potential, providing a mechanistic link between adaptation to environmental predators and survival in the human host.

papers.title: Water Kefir as a Model for Aggregative Development of Microbial Multicellularity within a Multispecies Biofilm
papers.abstract: Water kefir is a traditional fermented beverage and a non-dairy alternative to milk kefir. Water kefir grains are cauliflower-like aggregates, ranging in size from 1-20 mm. They are composed of an exopolysaccharide matrix derived from the fermentation substrate sucrose. The microbial community on and within the grains is a complex, highly stable multicellular aggregate typically consisting of 10-15 core species that primarily belong to three major groups: lactic acid bacteria, acetic acid bacteria, and yeasts. Remarkably, the structural organisation, stability, and growth of kefir grains cannot be readily explained by their constituent species alone, and attempts to reconstitute them from the isolated species have so far been unsuccessful. Here, we combined a comprehensive structural investigation of the macro- and micromorphology of water kefir grains with culture-dependent and -independent analyses of its microbial biodiversity. The dynamics and interactions within this complex microbial community were studied by combining flow cytometry, fluorescence-activated cell sorting, and amplicon sequencing of selected subpopulations. Furthermore, the growth of water kefir grains was spatiotemporally resolved and quantitatively characterised, thereby unravelling an emergent multicellular growth function, documented for the first time. Our combined evidence provides an unprecedented understanding of a highly structured and metabolically synergistic multicellular microbial aggregate and lets us propose water kefir as a model system for the aggregative development of microbial multicellularity from multiple species. It should lay the foundation for future mechanistic studies aimed at understanding how multispecies microbial communities self-organise into stable, spatially structured multicellular aggregates.

papers.title: Staphylococcus aureus GpsB, Stk, and VraSR form a cell wall surveillance network to maintain cell envelope integrity and mediate antibiotic resistance
papers.abstract: Antibiotic resistance is an alarming threat to public health worldwide. Specifically, drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus remains a major contributor to global mortality. Therefore, in-depth understanding of antibiotic resistance mechanisms is urgently needed to inform alternative therapeutic strategies. We previously showed that GpsB is a critical regulator of cell wall synthesis in S. aureus. GpsB executes its regulatory role via protein-protein interactions. Yet, how GpsB function is modulated in this organism has remained unclear. Intriguingly, a prior proteomics report indicated that GpsB is phosphorylated at six different residues by the sole serine/threonine kinase Stk. Hence, we explored the physiological significance of GpsB phosphorylation. We identify three phosphosites that are each independently sufficient to drive GpsB phosphoregulation, which likely alters its partner preference. We find that cells lacking gpsB exhibit heightened fosfomycin sensitivity, and that this is exacerbated by stk deletion. Our findings reveal that GpsB collaborates with Stk and the VraSR cell wall stress response system to coordinate the demand-driven availability of cell wall precursors. Collectively, this report establishes GpsB as a pivotal peptidoglycan supply chain sentinel that together with Stk and VraSR forms an integrated cell wall stress monitoring network that maintains cell envelope homeostasis and aids in antibiotic resistance.

papers.title: Urban Vietnam at the microbiome transition: Co-existing enterotypes reflect the global industrialization patterns
papers.abstract: Vietnam's rapid socioeconomic and dietary transition offers a rare window into how industrialization is reflected in the gut microbiome, yet Vietnamese populations remain underrepresented in global reference datasets. We investigated whether healthy Vietnamese adults in Hanoi harbor microbial community configurations associated with different stages of industrialization. Metagenomic data from stool samples of 183 clinically screened participants in Hanoi were analyzed alongside 629 publicly available metagenomic datasets from populations in low to middle income (LMI) and high income (HI) countries. Species-level taxonomic composition and gene-content-based metabolic pathways were characterized using community clustering and multivariable association analyses. Rather than forming a single population profile, the Vietnamese cohort separated into two enterotypes that mirrored the global industrialization gradient. Enterotype 1 more closely resembled populations from LMICs and showed greater microbial richness and diversity, whereas Enterotype 2 aligned with taxonomic and functional profiles observed in HICs. Both taxonomic and functional potential shows similar trajectories. Diet and lifestyle patterns describe some of the variance between enterotypes, supporting an association between contemporary exposures and microbiome structure without establishing causation. Antibiotic resistance profiles also varied between enterotypes, suggesting that the transition may encompass functions relevant to antimicrobial exposure. Together, these findings position urban Vietnam at a microbiome transition, where community states associated with different levels of industrialization coexist within a single population. This Vietnamese reference cohort expands representation in global metagenomic research and provides a baseline for tracking how rapid socioeconomic change may reshape microbial ecology, metabolic capacity, and antimicrobial resistance.

papers.title: Widespread attraction of marine bacteria to the macroalgae-derived polysaccharide fucoidan
papers.abstract: Fucoidan is the second most abundant polysaccharide in brown macroalgae, contributing up to 50% of the dissolved organic matter released daily from these algae into the ocean, substantially influencing the marine carbon cycle. Due to its complex chemical structure, fucoidan is highly resistant to microbial degradation and accumulates on the surface of macroalgae, where it contributes to regulating their microbiome. Here, we used a range of microfluidic assays to quantify the chemotactic and physiological responses of marine bacteria to fucoidan. Our results reveal that all the strains tested (14 out of 14) are attracted to fucoidan produced by two different species of brown macroalgae. Attraction occurred only at high fucoidan concentrations (0.1 to 1 mg/mL), such as those expected in the immediate vicinity of algal surfaces, whereas low concentrations elicited no response or modest chemorepulsion. Although fucoidan did not support bacterial growth under our experimental conditions, it did not impair the utilization of other carbon sources. Together, these findings suggest that fucoidan gradients can act as chemical cues guiding marine bacteria toward the nutrient-rich microenvironment of macroalgal surfaces, pointing to a potential ecological role of fucoidan in shaping macroalgal microbiota, bacterial behavior, and ultimately carbon cycling in the ocean.

papers.title: Complete ammonia-oxidizing Nitrospira and ammonia-oxidizing archaea as biological supplements for freshwater aquaria
papers.abstract: Biological filtration in newly established aquaria depends on the establishment of nitrifying microorganisms that prevent accumulation of toxic ammonia and nitrite. Many aquarists use commercial nitrifying supplements to accelerate biofilter establishment and reduce ammonia and nitrite accumulation. However, the microbial composition and in situ efficacy of these products remain poorly characterized. We evaluated the ability of enrichment cultures containing comammox Nitrospira (CX) and the ammonia-oxidizing archaeon Ca. Nitrosotenuis aquarius (AQ) to serve as aquarium nitrifying supplements, tested alongside a conventional supplement (CS) containing ammonia-oxidizing bacteria. Inoculation of new aquaria containing zebrafish (Danio rerio) with nitrifying supplements resulted in distinct nitrifier profiles within biofilters of each treatment group corresponding with significant reductions in peak ammonia and nitrite concentrations, which were most evident when applied at the maximum tested supplement dose. Treating aquaria with CX, AQ, or CS maintained ammonia and nitrite at low concentrations, and CX effectively prevented ammonia and nitrite accumulation through all stages of aquarium operation and biofilter establishment. After removing all fish from the aquaria, ammonia "spike-in" experiments demonstrated biofilters treated with CX and AQ conferred long-term protection against nitrite accumulation following acute ammonia loading events. Whereas 16S rRNA gene sequences associated with CS were rarely detected within biofilter profiles, those associated with CX and AQ established early and persisted temporally. Overall, results demonstrate how nitrifiers might be differentially adapted to home aquarium conditions and the potential of AOA and comammox Nitrospira to improve biofilter establishment and maintaining safe water quality in newly established freshwater aquaria.

papers.title: AMMPER-2: A spatially explicit agent-based model of microbial radiobiology with redox dye simulation
papers.abstract: To reduce health risks for human space exploration, it is important to model the effects of deep-space radiation on biological systems. The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a common model organism in space radiobiology, but little is known about how radiation damage to individual cells translates into the population-level effects that experiments measure. The Agent-Based Model for Microbial Populations Exposed to Radiation (AMMPER) is a spatially explicit agent-based model that simulates the effects of ionizing radiation on S. cerevisiae cells and produces population-level results. Its goal is to improve experiment design and data interpretation. AMMPER-1 demonstrated that agent-based simulations can qualitatively reproduce the effects of proton radiation on the growth rate of wild-type and DNA-repair mutant yeast. Here, we present AMMPER-2, which addresses limitations of the first model and expands its capabilities. AMMPER-2 incorporates the dynamics of the redox dye alamarBlue, a data type commonly generated in spaceflight microbiology experiments, and models the fate of reactive oxygen species in more detail. It also adds an improved graphical interface and runs faster. AMMPER-2 remains easy to execute in Python on a standard personal laptop, providing space biologists a tool to explore experimental conditions, generate hypotheses, and interpret data from microbial space radiation experiments.

papers.title: A domesticated prophage enzyme links bacterial metabolism, episymbiosis and phage fitness
papers.abstract: Prophages are increasingly recognized as drivers of bacterial adaptation, yet how domesticated prophage genes shape microbial symbiosis remains poorly understood. Here, we identify GDPDXhp1, a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase encoded by prophage Xhp1 of Schaalia odontolytica XH001, as a metabolic regulator linking bacterial physiology, episymbiosis and phage fitness. Association with the epibiotic bacterium Nanosynbacter lyticus TM7x strongly induced gdpdXhp1 expression and triggered GDPDXhp1-dependent lipid droplet accumulation in XH001. GDPDXhp1 orchestrated glycerophospholipid remodeling, membrane biophysical properties, respiration and cell-surface glycan composition in XH001, thereby promoting TM7x episymbiosis. Remarkably, GDPDXhp1 was also required for productive Xhp1 infection by remodeling susceptible bacterial host envelope structures to facilitate phage-host interactions. Together, our findings reveal a domesticated prophage enzyme that contributes to bacterial metabolism, interspecies symbiosis and viral reproduction, highlighting prophage as an overlooked source of metabolic innovation in microbial symbiosis.

papers.title: A niche-specific role for ArlRS enables Staphylococcus aureus growth within Kupffer cells
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections cause severe morbidity and mortality despite antibiotic therapy. We previously identified Kupffer cells (KCs) as the primary hepatic macrophages that rapidly clear circulating S. aureus, yet a subset of bacteria survives intracellularly and seeds systemic infection. Here, using spinning-disk intravital and super-resolution microscopy, we show that bacterial two-component system (TCS) signaling is required for intracellular replication within KCs in vivo. A global mutant lacking all non-essential TCSs failed to form intracellular microcolonies, and targeted analysis identified the ArlRS system as specifically required for KC replication. {Delta}arlRS bacteria remained as single non-replicating organisms within KCs, exhibited reduced dissemination and kidney abscess formation, and showed attenuated virulence with improved host survival. Complementation with arlRS restored the wildtype phenotype. Notably, the intracellular replication defect was not observed in primary or cultured macrophages, indicating that ArlRS-dependent replication is highly niche-specific and not reproduced by conventional in vitro models. Furthermore, restricting the KC reservoir with vancomycin treatment after infection further reduced renal infection by {Delta}arlRS bacteria. These findings identify ArlRS as a critical regulator of intracellular replication within KCs and establish the KC intracellular reservoir as a key driver of S. aureus pathogenesis and a potential therapeutic target during bloodstream infection.

papers.title: Label-free identification of bacterial species using adapted vision transformers
papers.abstract: Antibiotic resistance is an increasingly serious problem worldwide. Identifying the bacterial species can help guide antibiotic selection and improve patient outcomes. In sepsis, where every minute counts, rapid identification is particularly important, and new approaches are needed. In this study, deep learning models were trained to identify bacterial species from phase-contrast time-lapse images of cells growing in microfluidic traps, without fluorescent labels. We demonstrated this approach in two previous studies using laboratory strains. Here, the previous work is extended to clinical bacterial isolates, evaluating performance on isolates not seen during training. Furthermore, it was tested whether autofluorescence could aid species identification. Two validation sets were acquired in separate experiments from the training data, the first containing clinical-isolate traps with five species (Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus and Enterobacter cloacae), imaged every two minutes, and the second containing clinical isolates of two species (E. coli and K. pneumoniae) recovered from spiked donor blood, imaged every minute. Training with the best previous CNN method achieved unsatisfactory results. Therefore, vision transformers were explored, and a self-supervised adaptation procedure was developed for pretrained DINOv3 using a frozen teacher, followed by supervised classification using time-lapse montages. Mean macro-F1 was 93.6 {+/-} 1.3% for isolates precultured in Mueller-Hinton medium using 60 frames (118 minutes) and 87.2 {+/-} 2.7% for isolates precultured in blood using 55 frames (54 minutes) (mean {+/-} sample standard deviation across training seeds). Performance was evaluated over time by increasing the number of frames available to the model during testing, and Fourier-domain filtering approximated reduced numerical aperture. The results are promising and suggest that the aperture can be decreased while retaining good results. However, further evaluation on independent isolates, experiments and patient samples is needed to establish generalization. Together with previous findings, these results bring us closer to rapid image-based diagnostics that could transform the initial treatment of acute bacterial infections by enabling better-informed antibiotic selection.

papers.title: Metagenomic insights into dose-dependent alterations in the tobacco rhizosphere microbiome by pyrroloquinoline quinone
papers.abstract: Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) is known to promote plant growth, yet how the rhizosphere microbiome varies with PQQ concentration remains poorly understood. We applied metagenomic sequencing to characterize the taxonomic composition and functional potential of the tobacco rhizosphere microbiome across PQQ treatments at 0.5, 1 and 2 mol/L plus an untreated control. The rhizosphere microbiome was dominated by Pseudomonadota and Actinomycetota and differed among treatments in a concentration-associated, non-monotonic manner. The most pronounced differences were observed at 1 mol/L, where alpha diversity showed dimension-specific variation and beta-diversity analysis resolved the most distinct community profile. Taxonomic and functional profiles varied concurrently, with Streptomyces, Sphingomonas, Rhodanobacter and Lysobacter, together with functions related to biosynthesis, energy metabolism, colonization and environmental sensing, showing higher relative abundance at this concentration. No broad-spectrum antimicrobial effect was detected at the community level, and antibiotic resistance gene abundance showed no significant differences among treatments after correction for multiple testing. These findings provide a basis for further evaluation of PQQ in modulating the rhizosphere microbiome in continuous cropping systems.

papers.title: HIV remodels germinal centers through T follicular helper cell loss
papers.abstract: T follicular helper cells (Tfh) within germinal centers are among the most permissive cells for HIV infection and serve as a critical part of the viral reservoir. Given the key role of Tfh in affinity maturation and the production of plasma cells and memory B cells, an understanding of this critical viral reservoir is fundamental not only for cure strategies but also for understanding immunodeficiency in people living with HIV (PLWH). Using rare clinical specimens from PLWH, we demonstrate that HIV causes both a change in the cellular composition of germinal centers and changes in their overall architecture in ways that are consistent with the immunodeficiency seen in PLWH, independent of their CD4 count. We note a significant decrease in the number of GC Tfh cells and an increase in the number of follicular CD8 T cells in lymphoid tissues obtained from PLWH. Our data further show that GC size is decreased both by HIV and with increased age. Single-cell RNA sequencing data demonstrate that HIV acutely decreases the expression of Tfh B-cell support pathways and disrupts Tfh expression of cell trafficking receptors. Additionally, in a lymphoid organoid model of acute infection that forms GC-like structures, these findings are recapitulated, suggesting that New Approach Methodologies could be germane to understanding the impact of HIV on the reservoir and immunodeficiency. This study describes previously undocumented remodeling of the germinal center niche in PLWH, providing insight into the immune microenvironment of a key HIV reservoir that may help inform future cure strategies.

papers.title: Type 6 secretion systems of adherent-invasive Escherichia coli isolated from Crohn's disease patients shape intestinal microbiota.
papers.abstract: Adherent Invasive Escherichia coli (AIEC) colonize the ileal mucosa of Crohn's disease patients. Among bacterial virulence factors potentially implicated, type 6 secretion systems (T6SS) are molecular machineries sending effectors in prokaryotic or eukaryotic target cells. Two T6SS have been reported in AIEC LF82 reference strain. Here, we show that T6SS genes are more prevalent in Crohn's disease patients' microbiota compared to healthy controls, and that T6SS are more frequent in AIEC pathovar compared to E. coli in general and associated with FimH pathoadaptive polymorphism. The use of an in vitro gastrointestinal system coupled with T6SS promoter reporter assay highlighted expression of LF82 T6SS under gastrointestinal conditions, with a major role for bile salts. In mice infected with AIEC LF82 versus T6SS-deleted mutants, T6SS showed a functional impact in modulating the composition of mucosa-associated gut microbiota. Thus, AIEC may use their T6SS to compete with endogenous microbiota to colonize host mucosa.

papers.title: Targeted Depletion of rRNAs and Tobamoviruses Enhances Viral Discovery in Wastewater Metatranscriptomes
papers.abstract: Wastewater contains a complex mixture of nucleic acids derived from human cells, microorganisms, diets, and agricultural or industrial inputs. Metatranscriptomics has the potential to broaden the understanding of wastewater viromes, but its utility is constrained by high-abundance RNA molecules that prevent the detection of lower-abundance signals, including human pathogens. Two major sources of this interfering background signal are ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) from various organisms, and plant-infecting tobamoviruses from human diets, which are often the most abundant RNA viruses in wastewater. These rRNA molecules and RNA genomes can account for upwards of 95% of total RNA sequences, thereby obscuring the detection of lower-abundance viruses of public health importance. This study evaluated whether combined depletion of ribosomal RNAs and genomic RNA from abundant plant tobamoviruses can improve the recovery of underrepresented viral sequences from wastewater. RNA extracts from a large municipal wastewater treatment plant in Calgary, Canada, were processed with or without probe-based depletion of rRNAs and eight abundant tobamoviruses. Metatranscriptomes revealed that depletion reduced rRNA reads by 90%. Reads assigned to tobamoviruses, which accounted for up to 25% of viral reads in untreated samples, were reduced to <2% of viral reads after depletion. This decrease in undesired RNA signal led to an order of magnitude increase in viral read signals and improved assembled viral genome quality. Furthermore, the number of reads assigned to human and animal pathogens increased 42-fold after depletion, enabling the detection of important pathogens like influenza, RSV, and hepatitis A, which were undecteable in untreated samples. Together, these findings demonstrate that targeted depletion of abundant background RNAs improves the detection of low abundance viruses, and enhances the utility of metatranscriptomic approaches for wastewater viral surveillance.

papers.title: Genomic signatures of coevolving phage-bacteria interaction networks
papers.abstract: In diverse natural communities, cells and phages interact with many potential partners, but the impacts of pairwise coevolution on the overall structure of phage-bacteria interaction networks (PBINs) is not fully understood. Here, we conducted multiple pairwise coevolution experiments and examined how coevolution with one partner could simultaneously influence interactions with other partners. We then analyzed the underlying genetic changes that alter interactions in a large cross-experiment PBIN. The results reveal that interactions at the cell surface as well as intracellular interactions can alter patterns across the PBIN. When phages utilized the same set of host cell-surface receptor genes, pairwise coevolution with one partner did alter interactions with other partners. In contrast, if different sets of host cell-surface receptor genes were used, modular patterns in the cross-experiment PBIN were generally observed. On the phage side, resistance-breaking mutations arose in many putative receptor-binding proteins, and these changes could alter interactions with other hosts. However, in both the hosts and phages, over half of the mutated genes were not associated with cell-surface interactions. Host mutations likely altering intracellular phage-host interactions, including translation, protein stability, and DNA replication often led to broad resistance across the PBIN. In phages, mutations occurring in genes encoding endolysins, DNA methylases, oxygenases, transcriptional regulators, and tRNAs were observed potentially also influencing intracellular interactions. Based on these results, we propose a model to illustrate how these two different types of genetic signatures (i.e. extracellular cell-surface interactions verses intracellular interactions) can impact the structure of PBINs.

papers.title: The proteasome and ERAD pathways can regulate hepatitis E virus pORF1 proteostasis and genome replication
papers.abstract: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a major cause of acute viral hepatitis, with an estimated 20 million human infections annually. Its diverse host range presents a significant zoonotic threat, yet the molecular mechanisms underpinning HEV-host interactions remain poorly characterised. Here, we used transposon-based insertion screening of the HEV pORF1 polyprotein to identify a novel region within the viral PCP domain that permits HA-epitope insertion, enabling the first epitope tagging of this domain. Combined with V5 tagging of the hypervariable region (HVR), this approach enabled the generation of a replication-competent stable cell line expressing dual-tagged ORF1. Co-immunoprecipitation and TMT-based LC-MS proteomics revealed that pORF1 interacts with host proteins involved in endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) and the 26S proteasome. Pharmacological inhibition demonstrated that both pathways are required for efficient HEV replication. Treatment with the FDA-approved proteasome inhibitor bortezomib altered pORF1 precursor abundance and led to loss of full-length pORF1 through enhanced proteolysis. Importantly, the kinetics of ORF1 degradation following proteasome inhibition correlated with immediate loss of HEV replication, demonstrating a functional link between pORF1 proteostasis and viral replication. Collectively, our findings identify the ERAD network as a previously unrecognised requirement for HEV replication and establish a role for the 26S proteasome in maintaining pORF1 proteostasis.

papers.title: Coronavirus spherules are supported by a novel triple-layer protein lattice
papers.abstract: Coronaviruses (CoVs) cause significant disease in humans and animals, with a track-record of cross-species transmission. Despite their global significance, available control strategies are limited, especially for emerging CoVs. A deeper fundamental understanding of the virus life cycle is essential to underpin development of control measures. A critical step of the CoV life cycle is the rearrangement of host cell membranes into replication organelles (ROs). This is conserved across all CoVs and ROs comprise double membrane vesicles (DMVs), the site of viral RNA synthesis, and double membrane spherules. CoV spherules are complex structures requiring both positive and negative curvature of paired membranes so are predicted to have a high energy cost to maintain. To date they have an entirely unknown function. Interestingly, although always present, abundance of spherules in CoV infected cells varies with Betacoronavirus Middle East Respiratory Syndrome coronavirus, Gammacoronavirus infectious bronchitis virus (IBV) and porcine deltacoronavirus in particular producing a considerable number. Here, using cryo-bioimaging we identified for the first time that CoV spherules are embedded with a complex and organised triple-layered protein lattice and that spherules always contain a cargo that appears arranged as a shell inside the vesicle. In addition, we confirmed the presence of a double membrane spanning molecular pore in Gammacoronavirus DMVs and further identified a population of potential DMV formation intermediates. Together, this work provides a foundation for understanding a fundamental yet unresolved aspect of coronavirus replication.

papers.title: Regulation of PL fimbriae (plf) and role of PlfB as a negative regulator during avian pathogenic Escherichia coli infection in turkeys
papers.abstract: Little is currently known about the regulation of PL fimbriae produced by some pathogenic E. coli strains. We identified PlfB, a transcriptional regulator of the PapB family, as a negative regulator of PL fimbriae (Plf). Deletion of plfB significantly increased plfA transcription and Plf production. PlfB bound specifically to the plfA promoter region. Using a PplfA-lux reporter system, the deletion of plfB caused sustained and increased expression across serial passages. Global regulatory genes such as lrp, argR, and hns were also implicated in regulation of plf expression. Loss of lrp or argR decreased plf expression, suggesting these regulators positively regulate PL fimbriae. By contrast, loss of hns increased levels of plf expression, supporting its role as a negative regulator. Interestingly, loss of plfB significantly increased bacterial colonization in the lung of 6-day-old turkey poults. Further, complementation of plfB restored plf fimbrial expression and colonization of turkey lungs to wild-type levels. This further supports an important role for PL fimbriae for colonization of turkey lungs, since loss of plfB which resulted in increased plf gene expression in turkey lungs also correlated with higher bacterial numbers in the lungs. Taken together, these results indicate that PlfB acts as a negative regulator to reduce levels of PL fimbrial expression, under some conditions, but that it is not required for plf expression. This contrasts with the role the PapB regulator, which has been shown to play an essential role in expression of P fimbriae in uropathogenic E. coli strains.

papers.title: Strain handling exposes IS-mediated recurrent genome reduction at a dynamic accessory locus in Komagataeibacter rhaeticus
papers.abstract: Bacterial genomes are dynamic and harbour accessory regions that can be gained, lost, or rearranged in response to selective pressures. Members of the genus Komagataeibacter are used for bacterial cellulose production and researched as platforms for engineered living materials. However, their genomes are rich in mobile genetic elements (MGEs), including insertion sequences (ISs), genomic islands and prophage remnants, which drive genome rearrangements under agitated cultivation conditions. Whether this genome architecture contributes to genomic changes during routine strain maintenance and distribution remains poorly understood. Comparative genome sequencing of independent Komagataeibacter rhaeticus iGEM stocks revealed recurrent loss of a 210 kbp chromosomal region flanked by homologous IS5 sequences. This deletion was identified in a stock received as an agar stab and reproduced from an intact-genome population subjected to simulated agar-stab handling. Phylogenomic analysis of the affected locus revealed gene-tree/species-tree discordance, heterogeneous GC content and multiple ISs, supporting its characterization as a dynamic accessory region. Populations carrying the larger genome reduction showed improved growth and cellulose production relative to the intact genome reference, whereas populations carrying a smaller nested deletion showed reduced performance. These findings demonstrate that routine strain handling is not necessarily genomically neutral and can expose structural genomic variabilities that generate population-level genomic heterogeneity with phenotypic consequences. For bacteria with MGE-rich genomes, handling history may represent an underappreciated source of genomic and phenotypic variation between laboratories. More broadly, identifying unstable accessory regions may highlight genomic content that is dispensable under laboratory conditions, providing candidates for genome streamlining and strain improvement.

papers.title: Fecal Contributors to an Urbanized Estuary Identified by a Multi-Species qPCR Approach
papers.abstract: Coastal waters often experience fecal contamination from human (e.g., septic systems, wastewater treatment catchments and outfalls) and non-human (e.g., wildlife, domesticated pets, and livestock) origins, posing human health risks through contaminated fisheries and recreational waters. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) methods can identify and quantify fecal origins for their management by targeting Bacteroides, a dominant group of gastrointestinal bacteria with high host specificity. This study identified major contributors and drivers of fecal contamination to Mobile Bay, Alabama, an urbanized estuary in the southern United States. We utilized a multi-species qPCR source tracking approach targeting total Bacteroides and human-, pig-, dog-, cow-, and fowl-associated Bacteroides. Water samples and environmental parameters were collected over one year from 13 sites that represent a range of potential fecal inputs common to coastal waters. Human-associated feces were a consistent major contributor to the system (positive in 82% of samples), with localized inputs from pig (wild or domestic) and dog. Freshwater discharge and nitrogen constituents were good predictors of Bacteroides concentrations in this system, while areas with impervious surfaces and developed land cover may be contributing elevated fecal indicator levels. The multi-species qPCR source tracking approach described in this study can be implemented in other watersheds to support the development of better detection, identification, and fecal management strategies for community health of coastal areas.

papers.title: The ABC-F protein Uup, Rescues Stalled Ribosomal Termination Complexes to Modulate DNA Maintenance
papers.abstract: The cytosolic ATP-binding cassette F (ABC-F) family modulates ribosomal activity in eukaryotes and prokaryotes. Although they all bind to the E site of the ribosome, some bacterial ABC-Fs confer resistance to ribosome-targeting antibiotics, while housekeeping members have poorly defined roles. Interestingly, in Escherichia coli, which possesses four ABC-F (EttA, Uup, YbiT and YheS), Uup has been rather implicated in DNA recombination. Using an unbiased approach, we reconcile this apparent discrepancy by showing that Uup's involvement in DNA recombination is indirect and is dictated by Uup-mediated regulation of the last steps of translation that rescues problematic translation of genes involved in DNA maintenance such as ssb and dnaX. Accordingly, the elongated cell phenotype observed in uup deletion background is reverted by expressing a ssb variant that no longer depends on Uup. Unlike its paralog EttA, which helps ribosomes in translating proteins with repeats of negatively charged residues in the N-terminal 30 amino acids, Uup instead facilitates the rescue of stalled translation termination events that, in its absence, are handled by the tmRNA pathway.

papers.title: tRNA-derived second messengers confer bacterial immunity
papers.abstract: Bacterial small-molecule messengers that function in diverse immune signaling pathways have been thought to derive strictly from biosynthesis using nucleotide and cofactor substrates. Here we report a nuclease-driven immune signaling pathway in which tRNA cleavage generates a specific small molecule that triggers cell death in response to RNA-guided transcript recognition in prokaryotes. We identify a class of type VI-B CRISPR systems in which the RNA-guided nuclease Cas13 and its accessory transmembrane protein, 2TM{beta}, are co-encoded in an operon and are jointly required for bacteriophage defense. Upon target RNA recognition, Cas13 activates 2TM{beta} by producing mono- and dinucleotide messengers bearing 2',3'-cyclic uridine phosphate ends by tRNA cleavage. Activated 2TM{beta} destroys infected cells by forming a multimeric complex that disrupts cell membranes to mediate cell death. These findings demonstrate RNA-programmed tRNA cleavage for second-messenger biogenesis, revealing a new logic for prokaryotic immune signaling.

papers.title: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus Whole-Genome Diversity Reveals Divergence of Contemporary Populations in the United States
papers.abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) was introduced into the United States (USA) in 2013 and has circulated ever since. PEDV causes significant losses in the swine industry, with the greatest impact observed during the first years following its introduction into the country. However, the evolutionary dynamics of the virus remain underexplored. Recently, analyses of the Spike protein subunit S1 suggested that the PEDV population currently circulating in the USA represents a fraction of its historical diversity and comprises only two clades restricted to specific geographic regions. These observations were based on a limited set of S1 sequences. Furthermore, our understanding of evolutionary dynamics at the genomic level is even more limited, as complete PEDV genomes have not been generated since 2017. Here, we characterized the evolutionary dynamics of PEDV populations in the USA using complete genomes and assessed the contribution of different evolutionary mechanisms to shaping population structure. We analyzed 338 complete genomes, of which 25 were obtained in this study, together with 623 Spike S1 sequences, of which 41 were obtained in this study. All sequences obtained in this study were assigned to the non-S-INDEL strain. No S-INDEL sequences were recovered in this study, although these viruses continue to circulate in the country. Our analyses revealed that most sequences sampled after 2023 formed a monophyletic clade divergent from sequences collected in previous years, suggesting an ongoing temporal population structuring. Population structure analyses further supported evidence of population differentiation over time. Recombination analyses indicated that sequences belonging to the contemporary clade shared a single recombination event, suggesting that this clade may have emerged through recombination. Time-scaled S1 phylogenies were consistent with previous findings, supporting the circulation of only two contemporary clades; however, one of these clades was detected for the first time outside its previously reported geographic range. Our findings document temporal genetic differentiation in US PEDV populations, consistent with continued viral evolution, and broaden the known geographic distribution of contemporary S1 clades. These results highlight the value of continued genomic surveillance to monitor changes in PEDV diversity and distribution and provide sequence data to inform vaccine research.
